name: Read-Line Word Highlight
note: Splits each paragraph into word spans, then a scroll handler on the component's own overflow-y container compares cached word offsets against a reading line at 42% of the viewport, lighting every word above it and accenting the current one.
html:
The Long Read 0% read

Reading is a kind of scrolling that happened long before screens. The eye does not glide; it jumps, lands, fixes for a fraction of a second, then jumps again.

A page that lights each word as it passes the reading line is only making that rhythm visible. Nothing is added to the prose. The measure is simply drawn where the reader already is.

Set the line too high and the text feels chased. Set it too low and the highlight lags behind attention. Forty two percent down the column is close enough to honest.

End of excerpt · 3 min

name: Headline Mask Fill
note: A background-clip:text duplicate of the sticky headline is revealed with clip-path inset driven by a CSS scroll() timeline where supported, falling back to a scroll handler that writes the same progress custom property.
html:
Chapter 01 · Legibility

Make it readable at any speed Make it readable at any speed

0%

Type that survives a fast scroll is type with room around it. Weight alone will not save a line that has been packed edge to edge.

Fill the headline as the reader moves and the progress is felt rather than announced. The bar underneath is only there for the ones who count.

Stop the fill exactly where the section ends. A meter that reaches one hundred before the last line is a small lie the reader remembers.

html:
We spent the first year adding panels. Every request became a tab, every tab became a home for three more controls.

So we counted them. Nine decisions between opening the app and sending a single invoice, six of which the software could have made on its own.

The redesign removed four screens and shipped with fewer settings than the version it replaced. Support tickets fell by a third in the first month.

html:
Field notes — support triage 0%
reveal

01 — Intake

Every request lands in the same tray, unsorted, and sits there until somebody decides what it actually is. That decision is the whole product.

02 — Signal

We stopped counting messages and started counting resolutions. The graph went quiet and got far more honest with us.

03 — Drift

Six weeks in, the taxonomy had grown nine new labels. Nobody could name the person who approved a single one.

04 — Rewrite

So we deleted the labels, kept the traces, and let the shape of the work describe itself again.

end of notes

name: Spectrum Sweep Headline
note: A sticky headline is painted with an oversized background-clip:text spectrum whose background-position is animated by a scroll() timeline bound to the essay's own scroll container, falling back to a rAF-throttled scroll handler that writes the same --p custom property.
html:
Design in the open

Why the drafts stay public

The first version of every spec we write is wrong, and hiding it only delays the moment someone tells us so. Publishing the draft buys back a week.

We keep one document per decision. It opens with the call we made, then the alternatives, then the cost of being wrong. Nobody reads minutes; everybody reads a verdict.

What we stopped doing

We stopped writing status reports. The work already emits its own signal — commits, incidents, a changelog — and the report was mostly a translation layer for people who could have read the source.

We stopped inviting twelve people to a room to approve a change that two of them understood. Reviews now happen in the thread, in writing, where a decision can be quoted six months later.

The part that is hard

Working in the open means being visibly uncertain for longer than is comfortable. The trade is worth it: uncertainty shared early is cheap, and uncertainty discovered late is not.

Notes — Platform team, August
